# What is Quarto? {#sec-what-is-quarto}

[Quarto](https://quarto.org/) is a publishing system that lets you write formatted text (Markdown), code (Python, R, Julia) and the output of that code (figures, tables) together in a single document (`.qmd`). You then render that document to HTML, PDF or Word. This tutorial itself is written in Quarto.

For basic text formatting (headings, bold text, lists, links, ...) you use [Markdown](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/markdown-basics.html) syntax; the details of which will not be repeated here.

To get started, follow the installations instructions at [https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/)

# Previewing in VS Code

A basic intro to on how to use Quarto in VS Code can be found [here](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/hello/vscode.html#render-and-preview). The brief summary of the process is as follows:

1.  Install the [Quarto VS Code extension](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=quarto.quarto).
2.  With a `.qmd` file open, run the **Quarto: Preview** command (`Ctrl+Shift+K`, or the **Preview** button top-right of the editor) to render the document and open a live preview next to your source.


See [Render and Preview](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/hello/vscode.html#render-and-preview) for details. Note that VS Code is not the only way to interact with Quarto documents, as you can for example also use it from [RStudio](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/hello/rstudio.html).

# Python code blocks
A code block (*chunk*) starts and ends with three backticks, with `{python}` right after the opening backticks. Extra chunk options go on separate lines starting with `#|`, right at the top of the chunk. Type this yourself in a `.qmd` file:

````
```{{python}}
#| echo: true
import numpy as np

P = np.array([1.8, 2.1, 2.7, 3.4])  # [mm/d] precipitation
print(f"Mean precipitation: {np.mean(P):.1f} mm/d")
```
````

See the [full documentation](https://quarto.org/docs/computations/python.html) for all available chunk options. Rendered, the chunk above looks like this:

```{python}
#| echo: true
import numpy as np

P = np.array([1.8, 2.1, 2.7, 3.4])  # [mm/d] precipitation
mean_P = np.mean(P)
print(f"Mean precipitation: {mean_P:.1f} mm/d")
```

Before trying this yourself, make sure you have installed Python via Conda and configured it correctly, as outlined in the [Python and VS Code](python_vs_code.qmd) tutorial.

Additionally, it can also be useful to include variables from your Python code blocks in your text. For example, to include the numeric output of `mean_P` in your text, you can do so by adding ``{python} f"{mean_P}"``, where we use the so-called [f-string syntax](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/python/formatted-string-literals-f-strings-python/). This will then render as `{python} f"{mean_P}"`.

# Figures

All details on figures are in the [documentation](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/figures.html); labelling and referencing is explained under [cross-references](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/cross-references.html#figures).

## Imported figures

Insert an existing image with Markdown syntax. For a label (needed to reference it) and a caption, use:

```md
![A very scientific cat.](figures/quarto/cat.jpg){#fig-cat}
```

Rendered, this gives @fig-cat:

![A very scientific cat.](figures/quarto/cat.jpg){#fig-cat}

## Python figures

For a figure produced by Python code, set the label and caption as chunk options `label` (must start with `fig-`) and `fig-cap`:

````
```{{python}}
#| label: fig-precipitation
#| fig-cap: "Precipitation over time."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.plot(P)
plt.xlabel("Time (days)")
plt.ylabel("Precipitation [mm/d]")
```
````

Rendered, this produces @fig-precipitation:

```{python}
#| label: fig-precipitation
#| fig-cap: "Precipitation over time."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.plot(P)
plt.xlabel("Time (days)")
plt.ylabel("Precipitation [mm/d]")
plt.show()
```

## Referencing a figure

Reference a labelled figure anywhere in your text with `@fig-label`, e.g. `@fig-precipitation` gives @fig-precipitation.

# Tables

All details on tables are in the [Quarto documentation](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/tables.html); labelling and referencing is explained under [cross-references](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/cross-references.html#tables).

## Manual tables

Type a table directly in Markdown. Add a label (must start with `tbl-`) and caption on the line right after the table, preceded by a `:`:

```md
| Variable | Unit |
|----------|------|
| P        | mm/d |
| Q        | mm/d |

: Overview of the variables used {#tbl-variables}
```

Rendered, this gives @tbl-variables:

| Variable | Unit |
|----------|------|
| P        | mm/d |
| Q        | mm/d |

: Overview of the variables used {#tbl-variables}

## Python tables

For a table produced by Python code (e.g. a `pandas.DataFrame`), again use the chunk options `label` (starting with `tbl-`) and `tbl-cap`:

````
```{{python}}
#| label: tbl-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Summary of the precipitation data."
import pandas as pd

pd.DataFrame({"Mean": [np.mean(P)], "Sum": [np.sum(P)]})
```
````

Rendered, this produces @tbl-summary:

```{python}
#| label: tbl-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Summary of the precipitation data."
import pandas as pd

pd.DataFrame({"Mean": [np.mean(P)], "Sum": [np.sum(P)]})
```

## Referencing a table

Reference a labelled table with `@tbl-label`, e.g. `@tbl-summary` gives @tbl-summary.

# PDF output

As mentioned in @sec-what-is-quarto, your Quarto document can be rendered to different output formats. The default is HTML (aka web page format), which works out of the box with Quarto installed. 

For PDF output, you need to have a [LaTeX](https://www.overleaf.com/learn/latex/Learn_LaTeX_in_30_minutes#What_is_LaTeX?) distribution installed on your computer. The easiest (and recommended) way do this is is to install [TinyTeX](https://yihui.org/tinytex/) by opening the command line and typing:
```
quarto install tinytex
```
You can subsequently check if the installation was successful by typing:
```
quarto tools
```
You should see a version (e.g. `v2026.09`) mentioned under `Installed` for TinyTex. For more info on PDF output in Quarto, see [the documentation](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/pdf-basics.html).
